items.text: Occupational burnout recovery means returning to previous performance. Autistic burnout recovery might mean never going back — because the way you were functioning before may be what caused it.
items.rationale: Names the core tension of autistic burnout without catastrophizing — gives permission to build something new rather than restore what was. The contrast with occupational burnout frames it cleanly for any reader.

items.text: Many autistic people mask their burnout the same way they mask their autism — keep showing up, keep performing. By the time the mask drops, the burnout is already severe. Shame is the mechanism that keeps it hidden.
items.rationale: Pins down 'I didn't know I was burning out' with real precision — not lack of self-awareness but the same masking mechanism that caused the burnout now concealing it. Quotable and specific.

items.text: Unmasking isn't a switch. A 2026 study models it as a slow, non-linear process that needs safety, time, and seeing other unmasked autistic people. You can't will it faster than your nervous system allows.
items.rationale: Directly counters the prescriptive 'just unmask' discourse with peer-reviewed framing. Reassures autistic adults who feel stuck mid-process that the difficulty is structural, not personal failure.

items.text: 'Pathological' describes demand avoidance from outside — through the eyes of people being refused. 'Persistent Drive for Autonomy' describes it from inside. Same reality. Completely different verdict.
items.rationale: Makes the PDA naming debate legible and personal without requiring any clinical background. The outside/inside contrast lands even for readers encountering this for the first time.

items.text: Late diagnosis grief and relief don't take turns. A 2026 study found they coexist and recur — you can feel both in the same afternoon, and one doesn't erase the other. That's not confusion. That's accurate.
items.rationale: Names the specific emotional texture people are living but rarely see articulated — simultaneous grief and relief as a recurring pattern, not a tidy sequence.

items.text: Getting a late diagnosis gives you language for your past. It doesn't automatically give you a new story about yourself. The rebuilding part takes longer, and almost nobody warns you about that.
items.rationale: Separates the immediate relief of having language from the longer identity reconstruction work — the 'belief' leg of the grief-relief-belief cycle that gets the least airtime.

items.text: AuDHD can mean building the routine your autistic brain needs and watching your ADHD brain dismantle it within a week. Then the shame. It's not a discipline failure. It's two systems in genuine conflict.
items.rationale: Goes past 'both conditions at once' to name the specific double bind — structure as both necessity and casualty. The shame callout is what makes it real rather than clinical.

items.text: Half-right in ADHD spaces. Half-right in autistic spaces. The AuDHD experience of not quite fitting either community's map is its own kind of lonely.
items.rationale: Short, punchy, instantly recognizable. Speaks to an experience without making a factual claim, so no sourcing needed. The compression is the whole point — this is the shareable version.

items.text: 68% of neurodivergent employees don't know what workplace accommodations they can request. Among those who did ask, 56% said it helped. The barrier isn't reluctance. It's information.
items.rationale: Leads with the striking stat and ends on a solvable frame. Works standalone and opens the door to follow-up content on specific accommodations without requiring it.
items.sensitivity_flag: Stats originate from Understood.org's 2025 Neurodiversity at Work survey, cited here via Simply Psychology 2026. Verify that the 68% and 56% figures trace cleanly to that primary source before posting.

items.text: For a PDA nervous system, offering a choice only works if the choice is real. The nervous system checks. It can tell the difference between genuine agency and a script that looks like choice. Fake options don't lower the threat response.
items.rationale: Addresses the specific failure mode of 'giving choices' that still don't work — a question parents and partners raise constantly — with precision rather than prescription.
items.sensitivity_flag: 'The nervous system checks' is community-facing metaphor, not a clinical mechanism claim. Acceptable as written; would need a caveat if language were pushed toward physiological specificity.

items.text: Low-demand parenting and permissive parenting are opposites. Permissive means less support. Low-demand means reducing unnecessary pressure until the nervous system is calm enough to connect, learn, and cooperate.
items.rationale: Gives parents the exact language to answer a critique they face constantly — from family, teachers, clinicians — and explains the underlying logic in two sentences.

items.text: If you spent decades building an identity around the mask, who are you without it? That's not a rhetorical question. It's the actual work unmasking requires.
items.rationale: Reframes unmasking as an identity question rather than a behavioral shift — invites genuine reflection without prescribing an answer or closing down the conversation.
